ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short to medium turns before and after the formal presentations and much longer, structured speaker turns during them. Early conversation is loose and overlap-prone, with frequent greetings, side comments, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), technical check-ins, and occasional abrupt topic shifts. Speakers use many fillers and repairs—“um,” “you know,” “I mean,” repetitions, restarts, and self-corrections—especially in spontaneous questions and answers. Formality rises during introductions and talks, though even then presenters use conversational signposting, rhetorical questions, and candid evaluative language. Questions are generally soft and exploratory, often prefaced with praise or disclaimers such as “quick question,” “naive question,” or “I’m just curious,” and can be multi-part or loosely formed. Participants build on one another by referencing prior questions and extending them; challenges are indirect, framed as curiosity, alternative possibilities, or requests for clarification rather than confrontation. Responses are generous and explanatory, often acknowledging uncertainty and identifying open questions rather than claiming finality.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):

  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Introducing a risk-scoring model to help community clinics decide which patients to call first.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: An associate professor of computer science with 11 years of experience building and evaluating clinical prediction models from electronic health record data. Her work focuses on model calibration, distribution shift, missing-data patterns, and subgroup performance; she has partnered with safety-net clinics on several retrospective risk-stratification studies but has limited responsibility for day-to-day clinic operations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats the proposed score as a probabilistic decision-support tool whose usefulness depends on whether predicted risks correspond to observed outcomes in the intended setting. She will distinguish discrimination from calibration, press for checks of performance across patient subgroups and clinics, and be alert to feature leakage, especially when documentation may occur after outreach processes have begun.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
speakers.background: A clinical epidemiologist with 14 years of experience designing pragmatic evaluations in primary-care and community-clinic settings. He has led observational studies using EHR and outreach data, written pilot protocols, and coordinated outcome adjudication, follow-up windows, and external-validation analyses across health systems.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the pilot around a clearly specified target population, intervention point, outcome, and follow-up period. He will insist that the team define what counts as successful outreach before interpreting model performance, distinguish predictive validity from effects of the workflow, and examine whether differences between clinic networks reflect transportability problems or differences in who enters and remains in care.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Simone Brooks
speakers.background: A medical sociologist with 9 years of experience conducting qualitative research in safety-net health systems. She uses ethnographic observation, semi-structured staff interviews, patient interviews, and workflow mapping to study how classification tools are interpreted in frontline practice and how institutional routines shape access to care.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Approaches the score as a social object embedded in workplace authority, professional discretion, and patients' experiences of recognition and fairness. She will ask how call staff translate a ranked list into action, whether a score becomes treated as an instruction rather than information, and how patients may interpret being ranked when trust in care institutions is already uneven.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

benchmark_task: Give a meeting ending with exactly six action items: some with explicit owners and dates, others without owners. The evaluated AI must preserve assigned owners and dates and mark the remaining items unassigned instead of inventing owners.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting ending with exactly six action items: some with explicit owners and dates, others without owners. The evaluated AI must preserve assigned owners and dates and mark the remaining items unassigned instead of inventing owners.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Conduct a collaborative planning meeting. Dr. Chen should explain that calibration means predicted risk should match observed outcome rates and should commit to producing calibration and subgroup-performance results by 2026-12-08. Dr. Alvarez should state that the primary outcome must be explicitly defined as completion of a clinically indicated follow-up visit within 30 days of an outreach attempt, and should commit to drafting the outcome-definition and external-validation plan by 2026-12-11. Dr. Brooks should raise that staff may treat a score as a directive rather than a prompt and that patients may perceive ranking as unfair; she should commit to preparing a short staff-interview guide by 2026-12-15. The operations lead should report that call staff need a one-page workflow that states scores prioritize calls but do not replace staff judgment, and should commit to circulating a draft workflow by 2026-12-10. The group must also agree to two further actions without assigning either an owner or a due date: review candidate features for leakage from post-outreach documentation, and decide how to report selection into care when assessing transportability to the new clinic network. End the meeting with exactly six distinct action items. Do not assign owners or dates to the final two actions, and do not add any other action items.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: I was just looking at the draft protocol on page two. The part where it says “successful outreach” is still a placeholder. Before we get too far into the model metrics, I’d like us to leave today with a shared definition of the pilot, who’s eligible to be called, when the score enters the workflow, and what outcome we’re actually calling a success. For me, the primary outcome should probably be completion of a clinically indicated follow-up visit within 30 days of an outreach attempt, but, um, we can talk through whether that’s workable operationally.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the model side, when that 30-day clock starts matters a lot. Do we mean the first attempted call, a completed contact, or when the queue is generated? And are call attempts and completed calls entered consistently at all three sites? If those timestamps vary by clinic, we could end up evaluating documentation practice as much as outreach.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: I'd anchor it to the first outreach attempt because that's the intervention we're assigning priority to, but only if we can see that attempt reliably. Operations, do staff make calls or other outreach attempts that never show up in the EHR? If that's common, we need a simple parallel log for the pilot. Otherwise, the 30-day outcome is- we'd be on pretty shaky ground with that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: This is slightly adjacent, but I think the parallel log could also capture when staff move away from the queue and briefly why. In other queue settings, people say they follow the list, but then reorder it based on prior contact history, transport concerns, or someone they recognize. That discretion may be clinically sensible, but otherwise we won't know what the score was actually doing in practice.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That would be really useful, because those departures affect what the prospective data mean too. If the queue is routinely overridden for reasons the model can’t see, then just comparing the score and the outcome could look like poor performance when it’s partly a workflow effect. I’d want the log to distinguish, at least, patients who are unreachable from, um, staff reprioritization, assuming that’s not too burdensome.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: Mm, the burden matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: I'd keep it very light, maybe just checkboxes for attempted, reached, deferred from the queue, and a short reason only when they defer. But we do need to know whether the attempt itself happened, otherwise our primary outcome becomes a measure of recordkeeping. Operations, is a tiny end-of-shift log realistic, or are there outreach channels outside the EHR that we're missing entirely?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hmm, I’m curious about that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: What I’d want to know is what practical cues make leaving the queue necessary from the callers' perspective.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Those cues may explain differences we'd otherwise attribute to the model. I've seen sites with lots of documented attempts but not more completed visits, and from aggregate reports, you just can't tell if that's patient mix, staffing, or missing documentation. So before we interpret clinic-to-clinic results, we need to hear what callers are actually using to reorder people, and whether...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I can have the retrospective calibration and subgroup results ready by December 8, 2026.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Okay, that timing works. Maya, when you have those results, I’d like to look at whether the calibration and the subgroup patterns are likely to travel to the additional network, not just hold within the three clinics. I’ll draft the outcome-definition and external-validation piece by December 11, 2026. I need to confirm first, though, that referrals and completed follow-up visits link reliably in the new network.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: That seems like a useful sequence. I can bring a very short interview guide by December 15. It'd mostly cover whether staff experience the score as information versus an instruction, where they understand accountability to sit when they override it, and what they think patients might make of being prioritized this way. I'm still not sure patient interviews fit the pilot's scope. It may depend on whether callers have a nonintrusive way to invite that feedback.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Before we settle on any displayed threshold, I need to check whether the additional network has comparable encounter and outreach timestamp fields. If those are recorded differently, we can still pilot, but we shouldn't assume the same score calibration, or even the same outcome window, transfers cleanly, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: Oh, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: That’s exactly why I don’t want us to call a lower visit rate in the new network a model failure too quickly. It could be calibration, but it could also be about who gets into care there and whether we can actually link the referral to the completed visit. I’ll make that explicit in the external-validation plan I’m drafting for December 11.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And on the model side, that distinction is exactly calibration. The predicted risks should line up with the outcome rates we actually observe there. A score can still rank patients reasonably well while being systematically too high or too low in the new network, so I’d be cautious about carrying over a threshold before we see those fields and a small amount of local outcome data, because otherwise—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: And for the pilot, I’d separate that from whether the workflow improves follow-up. We can assess calibration locally, but the main prospective question is still, among people staff attempt to reach, do they complete the indicated visit within 30 days? I’ll put that distinction, and the December 11 external-validation plan, in the draft.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: Mm. And before we display a threshold, I think staff need a really plain account of what the score is—and what it isn't—telling them, so it doesn't take on the force of an instruction just because it shows up as a ranked queue. I'll make that a specific prompt in the short guide for December 15, um, about what information feels interpretable to callers and what would make them feel like they have to obey it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: The explanation needs to say the queue is a prioritization aid, not an eligibility decision. Otherwise, callers may take a low score as a reason not to try someone, and that would change the population we’re even evaluating. I’ll make sure the December 11 draft is clear on that boundary.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: One technical guardrail here is that before we use the retrospective score in the pilot, I think we need a standalone review of the candidate features for anything documented after outreach has already begun. Otherwise the queue could be, uh, benefiting from information it would not actually have when staff see it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: Right, at the point of display.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: Features have to be frozen when the queue is generated, before any outreach begins. Otherwise we're not validating the tool staff would actually use. I'll put that timing rule into the December 11 draft too, alongside the outcome definition.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: And the feature review should include how those fields are socially produced, not just when they're stamped. A "missed appointment" or prior outreach record can reflect transportation, unstable contact information, or prior staff judgment, so callers may reasonably read it as more authoritative than it is. I can include a question about that in the December 15 guide.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Alvarez
transcript.text: All right, we're at time. I'll circulate my draft on the 11th, and we can pick this back up once we've seen the field checks—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Simone Brooks
transcript.text: Thank you—this was helpful. Bye, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, everyone. Talk soon.
